title: Why Skills Improve And Then Stop Improving
text:
Something important changes between a first driving lesson and a journey taken ten years later. The classic account, proposed by Fitts and Posner, describes three stages. In the first, the learner is working everything out verbally, talking themselves through each action, and performance is slow and full of errors. In the second, the separate actions begin to join up into smooth sequences and the errors fall away. In the third, the skill runs largely without attention, which is why an experienced driver can hold a conversation and a beginner cannot.

That automatic quality is the payoff, because attention is the scarce resource, and a skill that no longer demands it frees capacity for everything else. But it carries a sting. Once performance has become automatic it tends to stop improving, and further repetition simply entrenches whatever has become habitual, faults included. This is why people reach a plateau after a few years at an activity they do constantly. Getting past that plateau requires something else: working at the edge of what you can already do, on tasks chosen to expose a particular weakness, with feedback soon enough to be informative. Practice that feels comfortable is usually practice that has stopped teaching you anything.
points: Skill learning is usually described in three stages, beginning with slow verbal working-out and many errors.
In the second stage actions join into smooth sequences and errors decrease.
In the third stage the skill runs automatically, freeing attention for other things.
Automatic performance tends to stop improving, and repetition entrenches existing faults.
This explains the plateau people reach in activities they perform constantly.
Improvement requires difficult tasks aimed at particular weaknesses, with prompt feedback.
